subject: chemistry
pattern: Chemical Kinetics typically fetches 5-7 marks in the Karnataka 2nd PUC board paper: 1-mark order or molecularity, 2-mark pseudo first order or order vs molecularity, 3-mark numericals (half-life, Arrhenius, first order rate constant) and a 5-mark derivation of the integrated rate equation for zero or first order or the Arrhenius equation. Examiners expect the exact formula, log values, substitution and units.

questions.answer: The order of a reaction is the sum of the powers (exponents) of the concentration terms of the reactants in the experimentally determined rate law. For the rate law, rate = $k[A]^x[B]^y$, the overall order is $x + y$. It is determined experimentally, may be zero, fractional or whole number, and need not match the stoichiometric coefficients.
keywords: sum of powers of concentration terms

questions.q: What is meant by molecularity of a reaction?
questions.answer: Molecularity is the number of reacting species (atoms, ions or molecules) that must collide simultaneously in an elementary step to bring about a chemical reaction. It is always a whole number (1, 2 or rarely 3), is defined only for elementary reactions, and cannot be zero or fractional. Examples: unimolecular, bimolecular.

questions.q: Write the unit of rate constant for a zero order reaction and for a first order reaction.
questions.answer: For a general reaction of order n, unit of k = (mol L$^{-1}$)$^{1-n}$ s$^{-1}$. For a zero order reaction (n = 0), unit of k = mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$, same as the unit of rate. For a first order reaction (n = 1), unit of k = s$^{-1}$. The unit of k depends on the order of the reaction.

questions.q: Distinguish between order and molecularity of a reaction (any two points).
questions.answer: Order: (i) the sum of the exponents of concentration terms in the experimentally determined rate law; (ii) can be zero, fractional or a whole number; it applies to simple and complex reactions. Molecularity: (i) the number of reacting species colliding in an elementary step; (ii) always a whole number, never zero or fractional; applies only to elementary reactions. Order is determined experimentally while molecularity is theoretical.

questions.q: What is a pseudo first order reaction? Give one example.
questions.answer: A reaction that is bimolecular (or higher molecularity) but follows first order kinetics because one reactant is present in large excess, so its concentration remains practically constant, is called a pseudo first order reaction. Example: acid hydrolysis of ethyl acetate, CH$_3$COOC$_2$H$_5$ + H$_2$O $\to$ CH$_3$COOH + C$_2$H$_5$OH; water is in large excess, so rate = $k'[CH_3COOC_2H_5]$. Another example: inversion of cane sugar.

questions.q: The half-life of a first order reaction is 69.3 s. Calculate its rate constant.
questions.answer: For a first order reaction, $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$. Therefore $k = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{69.3\ \text{s}} = 0.01$ s$^{-1}$. The rate constant is $1 \times 10^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$.

questions.q: What is activation energy? Write the Arrhenius equation and explain the terms.
questions.answer: Activation energy ($E_a$) is the minimum extra energy that the reactant molecules must possess, over their average energy, to form the activated complex and change into products. Arrhenius equation: $k = A\,e^{-E_a/RT}$, where k is the rate constant, A is the frequency (pre-exponential) factor related to collision frequency and orientation, $E_a$ is the activation energy, R is the gas constant and T is the absolute temperature. The factor $e^{-E_a/RT}$ is the fraction of molecules with energy equal to or greater than $E_a$.

questions.q: Derive the integrated rate equation for a first order reaction.
questions.answer: Consider R $\to$ P. Rate = $-\dfrac{d[R]}{dt} = k[R]$. Rearranging, $\dfrac{d[R]}{[R]} = -k\,dt$. Integrating, $\ln[R] = -kt + I$ (I = constant). At t = 0, $[R] = [R]_0$, so $I = \ln[R]_0$. Hence $\ln[R] = -kt + \ln[R]_0$, or $k = \dfrac{1}{t}\ln\dfrac{[R]_0}{[R]}$. In common logarithm, $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[R]_0}{[R]}$. A plot of $\ln[R]$ against t is a straight line with slope $-k$.

questions.q: A first order reaction is 75 percent complete in 32 minutes. Calculate its half-life.
questions.answer: Let $[R]_0 = 100$, then $[R] = 25$ after t = 32 min. $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[R]_0}{[R]} = \dfrac{2.303}{32}\log\dfrac{100}{25} = \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.6021}{32} = 0.0433$ min$^{-1}$. Half-life $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.0433} = 16$ min. Thus the half-life is 16 minutes (75 percent completion needs two half-lives).

questions.q: The rate constant of a reaction doubles when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 310 K. Calculate the activation energy. ($R = 8.314$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$, log 2 = 0.3010)
questions.answer: $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)$. With $k_2/k_1 = 2$: $0.3010 = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303 \times 8.314}\times\dfrac{10}{300 \times 310}$. $E_a = \dfrac{0.3010 \times 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 93000}{10} = 53598$ J mol$^{-1}$, i.e. $E_a \approx 53.6$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

questions.q: A first order reaction has a rate constant of $1.15 \times 10^{-3}$ s$^{-1}$. How long will 5 g of this reactant take to reduce to 3 g?
questions.answer: $t = \dfrac{2.303}{k}\log\dfrac{[R]_0}{[R]} = \dfrac{2.303}{1.15 \times 10^{-3}}\log\dfrac{5}{3}$. $\log(5/3) = 0.2218$. $t = \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.2218}{1.15 \times 10^{-3}} = 444.2$ s. The time required is about 444 s.

questions.q: Explain collision theory of chemical reactions. What are effective collisions?
questions.answer: According to collision theory, a reaction occurs when reactant molecules collide. Rate = $Z_{AB}\,e^{-E_a/RT}$ with a steric (orientation) factor P included: $k = P\,Z_{AB}\,e^{-E_a/RT}$. Only a small fraction of collisions lead to products. Effective collisions are those in which (i) the colliding molecules have energy equal to or greater than the threshold energy, and (ii) they are properly oriented so that old bonds break and new bonds form. Other collisions are elastic and ineffective.

questions.q: Derive the integrated rate equation for a zero order reaction and obtain the expression for its half-life. Mention how the graph of [R] versus t looks.
questions.answer: For R $\to$ P of zero order, rate = $-\dfrac{d[R]}{dt} = k[R]^0 = k$. So $d[R] = -k\,dt$. Integrating, $[R] = -kt + I$. At t = 0, $[R] = [R]_0$, hence $I = [R]_0$ and $[R] = -kt + [R]_0$, or $k = \dfrac{[R]_0 - [R]}{t}$. Half-life: at $t = t_{1/2}$, $[R] = [R]_0/2$. So $k = \dfrac{[R]_0 - [R]_0/2}{t_{1/2}}$, giving $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[R]_0}{2k}$. Thus half-life is directly proportional to initial concentration. The graph of [R] against t is a straight line with negative slope $-k$ and intercept $[R]_0$.

questions.q: Explain the effect of temperature on the rate of a reaction using the Arrhenius equation. Derive the equation relating rate constants at two temperatures.
questions.answer: The rate constant of most reactions nearly doubles for every 10 K rise in temperature, because the fraction of molecules having energy greater than $E_a$ increases. Arrhenius: $k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}$. Taking ln, $\ln k = \ln A - \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$, or $\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303RT}$. A plot of $\log k$ against $1/T$ is a straight line with slope $-E_a/2.303R$. At $T_1$: $\log k_1 = \log A - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303RT_1}$; at $T_2$: $\log k_2 = \log A - \dfrac{E_a}{2.303RT_2}$. Subtracting, $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303R}\left[\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right] = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right]$.
keywords: fraction of molecules with energy >= Ea
